subject: Cognitive Science
title: Executive Function Development
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Executive Function Development.

hook.text: Tell a five-year-old new sorting rules. She keeps using the old ones—even though she knows they changed.

buildup.text: Executive functions include working memory, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility. They develop slowly.

discovery.text: These skills let you plan, resist impulses, and switch tasks. They underpin everything from math to manners.

twist.text: Executive function is a better predictor of school success than IQ. Self-control outpredicts smarts.

climax.text: Full maturity arrives in the mid-twenties. The last brain region to finish is the one you need most.

punchline.text: Self-control is the last upgrade installed.

quiz.question: What are the three core executive functions?

details.summary: Executive functions, including working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility, develop gradually through childhood and into the twenties. The prefrontal cortex, which supports these abilities, is among the last brain regions to mature.
details.whyItMatters: Executive function is the mental control system. Its slow development explains why children struggle with impulse control and why adolescents take risks despite knowing better.
takeaways: Includes working memory, inhibition, and flexibility
The prefrontal cortex matures into the mid-twenties
Executive function predicts school success and behavior

faq.question: Why can not young children control their impulses?
faq.answer: The prefrontal cortex responsible for inhibitory control is immature in young children. Neural connections are still forming, making it physically difficult to override prepotent responses. This is why toddlers grab toys despite being told not to; the hardware is not yet ready.

faq.question: Can executive function be trained?
faq.answer: Evidence suggests modest training benefits. Practice with working memory tasks, mindfulness, and certain curricula can improve performance, but gains do not always transfer broadly. The most effective approach combines direct training with supportive environments that reduce cognitive demands.
